entry.evidence: Despite efforts made in these studies, the gravity signature of the inter-seismic crustal dilatation and ETS events in western Canada remains unknown.

steps.action: The authors take from Mazzotti et al. and Lambert et al. an unexplained positive absolute-gravity trend of about 0.53 μGal/yr in southwestern British Columbia, not accounted for by vertical displacement.
steps.quote: They discovered an unexplained 0.53 μGal year−1 average rate of gravity change

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how continuous gravity changes relate to GPS-derived inter-seismic dilatation strain rates in the Cascadia Subduction Zone, including the effect of ETS events.
steps.quote: the relationship between gravity changes and dilatation strain rates in the CSZ is explored

steps.action: The iGrav superconducting gravimeter is chosen for its continuous sub-µGal precision; its portability and sensitivity were characterized in the authors' earlier tests at the University of Calgary.
steps.quote: Portability and sensitivity tests were conducted over the next six months, where an accuracy of better than 1 µGal was achieved

steps.action: The SG was deployed at PGC on Vancouver Island and recorded 1-s gravity from July 2012 to April 2015; it was calibrated by regression against parallel FG5-106 absolute gravimeter observations (Methods).
steps.quote: we deployed the iGrav® SG (serial number 001) at Pacific Geoscience Centre (PGC) in July 2012

steps.action: The authors reduce the record to residual gravity: tides and ocean loading with ETERNA, polar motion, frequency-dependent atmospheric admittance, GLDAS soil moisture calibrated to local sensors, and IDW-averaged vertical displacement at −0.2 μGal/mm (Methods 5.1). They then remove the 3.4 μGal coldhead-maintenance step, giving a trend of about 0.65 μGal/yr.
steps.quote: results in a total gravity trend of ~1.8 μGal or, equivalently, ~0.65 μGal year−1

steps.action: The corrections are checked: the PSD of raw versus tide-corrected signal shows the tides were removed, and a regression of rainfall against hydrology-corrected gravity shows a negligible residual rainfall effect.
steps.quote: Regression analysis between rainfall data and the hydrology-corrected gravity demonstrates negligible residual gravity effect of heavy rainfalls

steps.action: The −2.6 μGal step at the Haida Gwaii earthquake is checked against borehole strainmeters and hydrological sensors at PGC (no offset found), and the Craig earthquake is checked as well (no offset). The Haida Gwaii step is nonetheless kept in the signal rather than treated as an artifact.
steps.quote: There is no permanent offset observed in the BSMs, or other hydrological sensors in the vicinity of the PGC station

steps.action: Three ETS events (2012, 2013, 2014) are identified during the SG operation from PNSN tremor counts and detrended PGC5/BCNS GPS displacements, with about 5 mm and about 3 mm westerly movements.
steps.quote: Three major ETS events were distinguished from both tremor events and GPS data during the operation period of the SG at PGC.

steps.action: NGL velocities from 533 GPS stations are gridded into blocks, and strain and rotation rates are computed with GeoStrain least-squares collocation, giving horizontal dilatation of about −0.09 μstrain/yr at PGC.
steps.quote: show a maximum shortening rate of 0.13 μstrain year−1 southwest of the PGC and a 0.09 μstrain year−1 shortening rate calculated at PGC

steps.action: The GPS-derived horizontal shortening is compared with Cruikshank and Peterson's independent regional estimate of about 0.1 μstrain/yr.
steps.quote: Our GPS-derived horizontal dilatation is also confirmed by Cruikshank and Peterson46

steps.action: Vertical strain is estimated by dividing gridded vertical GPS velocity by the block depth (assuming negligible Moho motion) and added to horizontal dilatation, giving volumetric compression of about 0.07 μstrain/yr at PGC; uncertainties are propagated (Methods 5.3).
steps.quote: a ~0.07 μstrain year−1 compression was obtained at PGC (Fig. 5c)

steps.action: The authors compute the gravity expected from the volumetric dilatation with a Plouff rectangular-prism forward model (an improvement on Yin and Xu's Bouguer slab), using 2790 kg/m3 density, 45 km depth and a decoupled Moho. The result is about 0.4 ± 0.26 μGal/yr at PGC, and a feasibility test (Fig. 10) gives about 0.52 μGal for 0.1 μstrain.
steps.quote: The results indicate a maximum of ~0.43 μGal year−1 gravity change to the northwest of PGC while the gravity rate is ~0.4 μGal year−1

steps.action: The forward model is repeated for effective strain depths of 30 km (coupled Moho) and 55 km (strain in the subducting plate), giving maxima of about 0.37 and 0.47 μGal/yr.
steps.quote: we repeated the calculations for both 30 km and 55 km depths

steps.action: The SG trend of about 0.65 μGal/yr is compared with historical absolute-gravity trends of about 0.53 μGal/yr in the CSZ, and the increasing trend is attributed to accumulated inter-seismic strain.
steps.quote: has a good agreement with the historical absolute gravity trends (~0.53 μGal year−1) in CSZ

steps.action: Detrended eastward GPS displacement is compared with residual gravity across the three ETS cycles: a correlation of about −0.9, with gravity rising around ETS events and receding between them (Fig. 6, p. 8).
steps.quote: we found a meaningful negative correlation coefficient of ~−0.9 between the detrended eastward GPS data

steps.action: The 2014 event departs from the pattern: gravity rises weeks before the main ETS event, followed by a 4 μGal drop and recovery. The authors explain this with tremor maps (Fig. 7) pointing to a minor slip event near PGC, an auxiliary explanation rather than a revision of the claim.
steps.quote: can be evidence of a minor slip and can explain the timing of the rise in gravity signal before the main 2014 ETS event

steps.action: As an intuitive proxy for short-term directional strain, the authors difference the BCSM and SC02 GPS stations (east, north and subduction direction) and compare the result with gravity; relative compression increases around all three ETS events.
steps.quote: the relative movements increase during and around all three ETS events which represents a compression during these events and supports the gravity increase

steps.action: The coincidence of the Haida Gwaii earthquake with the 2012 ETS gravity peak is left as an open question for future study.
steps.quote: A more detailed investigation in future studies is necessary to find a possible link between the two events.

steps.action: The forward-modelled 0.4 ± 0.26 μGal/yr (45 km depth) is compared with the observed 0.65 ± 0.38 μGal/yr; the model falls short of the observation.
steps.quote: Gravity forward modelling predicts ~0.4 ± 0.26 μGal gravity increase due to the compression in a maximum depth of 45 km.

steps.action: The account is refined: the observed rate requires strain effective at greater depth, possibly mass accumulation in the subducting Juan de Fuca plate.
steps.quote: requires the shortening to be effective in a larger depth

steps.action: The claim is kept that the gravity increase reflects crustal compression from inter-seismic strain accumulation, with a significant part explained by the deformation model.
steps.quote: a significant part of the residual gravity of ~0.65 μGal year−1 can therefore be explained by the theoretical deformation model

tree.answer: Residual gravity increase of about 0.65 μGal/yr at PGC, 2012–2015
Gravity yes; the density change is not observed and is inferred from GPS strain through a forward model
Relate gravity change to inter-seismic dilatation strain and ETS
No stated rival explanations; environmental effects are corrected, not tested as rivals
Forward model predicts 0.4 ± 0.26 μGal/yr against an observed 0.65 μGal/yr
Conditions found: three ETS events in the live record

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats ETS cycles three times; gravity–eastward GPS correlation of about −0.9
Partly: depth sensitivity 30–55 km, station-difference GPS proxy, correction checks
Kept; partly explained, with deeper strain invoked to close the gap
Not assessed; peer review file not supplied

end.claim: The gravity increase observed at PGC (about 0.65 μGal/yr) results from a crustal density increase due to compression, mostly from inter-seismic strain accumulation during Juan de Fuca subduction, modulated by ETS events.

decisive_move.sentence: Forward-modelling the gravity effect of the GPS-derived volumetric dilatation (about 0.4 μGal/yr at PGC) is what turns the gravity trend and its correlation with GPS into a density-change explanation.

gates.evidence: Action: the SG was deployed to reveal gravity changes associated with earthquakes and ETS (§2 ¶1), which is a directed question rather than a stated hypothesis. Claim: the forward model (0.4 ± 0.26) could have disagreed with the observation (0.65 ± 0.38), but the uncertainties are wide and the shortfall is absorbed post hoc by invoking deeper strain (§4 ¶2). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data, and correction choices (maintenance step removal, keeping the Haida Gwaii step) were made after inspecting the record (§2 ¶2–3).

limits: No peer review file was supplied, although the paper states that reviewer reports exist; no review sequence is coded. No rival explanation for the gravity trend is stated and tested: hydrology, vertical displacement and instrument effects are corrected, not excluded as rivals, and Mazzotti et al.'s unknown deep or near-surface mass source is not addressed directly. The residual-gravity uncertainty is given as 0.5 μGal in §2 ¶2 but 1 μGal in §5.3 ¶1. The trend uncertainty (±0.38 μGal/yr) and the model uncertainty (±0.26) overlap widely. The deeper-strain refinement is post hoc (inference). How the GPS series was detrended before the −0.9 correlation is not stated, so part of the correlation may follow from detrending choices (inference). The Haida Gwaii step is kept without a stated test of its effect on the trend. Sub-claims: strain rates at PGC are estimate_with_resolution (0.09 ± 0.011 horizontal; 0.07 ± 0.025 volumetric); the forward-model gravity rate is estimate_with_resolution (0.4 ± 0.26 μGal/yr); the gravity–eastward-GPS relation across three ETS cycles is regularity_in_range (three events only). The composition trace_series is approximate: the record is a live, found series over three repeated ETS cycles rather than past traces, and natures_repetition partly fits the ETS sub-claim. The step-removal and calibration details rely on supplementary figures that were not supplied.

disagreements.target: Lambert et al. (2006); Mazzotti et al. (2007): unexplained absolute-gravity trend in southwestern British Columbia
disagreements.support: The SG trend agrees with the absolute-gravity trend and is attributed to crustal compression, while being treated as a larger local effect than the regional absolute-gravity estimate.
disagreements.quote: our estimated rate of iGrav’s gravity change is considered a local effect which is larger than the estimated absolute gravity representing the regional effect

disagreements.target: Common practice of a simple vertical-displacement gravity correction
disagreements.support: The modelled dilatation gravity effect reaches μGal-level inter-annual change in tectonically active regions, so a dilatation strain correction is recommended.
disagreements.quote: this study recommends the dilatation strain correction in geophysical studies which focus on detection of subtle changes in the gravity field

disagreements.target: Yin and Xu (2017) Bouguer slab model of dilatation gravity
disagreements.support: The slab model ignores vertical strain and assumes infinite extent, so the authors replace it with a finite-prism volumetric model.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, a more accurate gravity to strain ratio is slightly smaller than the Bouguer slab model.

disagreements.target: Bouguer slab model and previous studies of the soil-moisture admittance (0.042 μGal/mm)
disagreements.support: Regression of calibrated GLDAS soil moisture against iGrav residual gravity yields a smaller admittance of 0.038 μGal/mm.
disagreements.quote: This admittance factor is smaller than the 0.042 μGal mm−1 obtained from the Bouguer slab model and previous studies
